"LSJ had every oppurtunity to discuss this with all of yourselves and other
people respected in this news group. Who also have played this game since its
arrival not that that is a valid argument anyway."

The bulk of the new errata is the direct result of years and years of
discussion. LSJ simply did not make up these rulings out of whole cloth--they
came directly from the debate on this newsgroup. The Tomb, TB, Mind Rape, and
RTI fixes are all pretty much identical to at least a few of the proposed fixes
that were beaten to death on this group for the last few years. The WWEF
ruling was the result of some of the very first discussions on this newsgroup
from however many years ago (heck, I think Alan Kwan was a proponent of said
fix...). The Aggro rules and the Vote push rules have been discussed forever,
and harken back to the original intention of the rules. The IG ruling, again,
also harkens back to the original intention of the rules. The 2nd Tradition
ruling was supported by a 3 week, infinitely long thread just before the ruling
came out, as well as the original card wording. The only entirely arbitrary
rulings I can think of are the Rutors Hand fix (which exists to fix a huge
loophole in the rules, and does so pretty elegantly) and Fame (which was well
regarded as a completely busted card from pretty much day one, and although the
current Fame fix is pretty severe, it certainly fixes Fame abuse).

"What he did was not his JOB if he did his JOB he would not have gotton the
response he did."

It certainly was his job. LSJ is the WOTC official net representitive as well
as the head of the rules team. If it wasn't his job to do what he did, I am
hard pressed to think of what his job is to do.

"And no longer has any respect from me."

The horror. The horror.

"I also warned everyone also that this was a Flame so they had the choice to
ignore it!"

Good lord--who wants to ignore such a preposterous flame?

By making errata or rulings that haven't been discussed here, it catches
everyone flatfooted. Fame is one. I don't recall anyone mentioning that
Wake trumps Sleeping Mind prior to the ruling. Possibly errataing Wakes
hasn't been discussed in this group for, what, years? If it had been
known that such errata were eminent, perhaps there would have been discussion
of whether there was still a need for such errata, and of possible
alternative fixes.

It is moot now, but it might have been more prudent/courteous for LSJ to
send up a trial balloon in the newgroup for the more radical
errata/rewordings, so that other reasonable alternatives could be discussed.
As it was, the decisions (as all previous RTRs have been before as well
-- so I'm not trying to pick on LSJ here) were delivered in a
take-it-or-leave-it manner. This RTR is such a major change to the current
game (D actions, agg damage, vote push, major errata to several cards)
that a totally new approach to the RTR process -- issuing an initial
provisional RTR for discussion -- might have been called for (this is
actually similar to method of creation of Internet standards -- the initial
issuance of an RFC [request for comment]). Then after that "provisional"
trial-balloon RTR, LSJ could issue a final RTR that keeps or changes things
as per LSJ's best judgement, but that also discusses why other specific
alternatives were rejected. That might have reduced the "anger level"
somewhat by giving people a feeling that they have some input into the
process at least.

I actually largely favor the 7/7 RTR. My differences with it are largely
quibbles (Fame, Sleeping Mind, agg damage). The true major drawback will
the difficulty of tournament organization at conventions. In this area
(the SF Bay area), getting information as extensive as the 7/7 RTR to
convention attendees before their arrival at the convention is essentially
impossible (if they aren't on the net). Obviously, having people arrive
at a Jyhad tourney with decks built for radically different rules sets
isn't going to be a pleasant experience. We'll just have to see how this
sorts out.

Messages.Author: Lupus Australis
Messages.Body:
On 4 Aug 1998, Eric Pettersen wrote:

> I don't recall anyone mentioning that Wake trumps Sleeping Mind prior to
> the ruling.

This one actually makes perfect sense to me, such that I don't even
necessarily consider it errata. It is merely a literal interpretation of
card text. I don't know if I discussed it on the net, but I have always
felt that this should have been the ruling.

the relevant text of Sleeping Mind says that "...tapped minions cannot
block this action."

This essentially takes away from them an ability that they do not have.
Tapped minions cannot normally block actions anyway. I imagine if some
hypothetical vampire had card text stating "this minion can attempt to
block even if tapped" then Sleeping Mind would take that power away.
Otherwise, null effect. It deprives them of the power if they have it,
but does not prevent another card from giving them that power later.

A wake played after Sleeping Mind restores what Sleeping Mind took away
(even if you never had it to begin with--which is always the case
with the current cardset).

Obviously, this is not what the card intended, as the final clause
otherwise becomes pointless with cards currently in print. Still, it is a
perfectly acceptable literal interpretation of what otherwise would be an
overpowered card.

This argument assumes that the card was intended to do nothing. I
think the general rule for cards that would do nothing if you read
them a certain way is to assume that they break the rules such that
they do something. (ex: Cat's Guidance, under the current rulings,
is played after the block finishes, which is after combat now, which
is clearly after the blocking vampire taps. However, it doesn't have
card text saying 'playable by a tapped vampire.' Nonetheless, it
is playable by a tapped vampire, because otherwise it would be
useless. At least, if I remember right, this is how LSJ's reasoning
went.)

The inferior of Sleeping Mind is 'Choose a tapped vampire.
The chosen vampire cannot attempt to block this action.' If Sleeping
Mind isn't meant to prevent Wakes/Forced Awakenings from circumventing
it, it is an inherently useless card.

As far as I can see, the only reasonable way to interpret the 7/7
errata to Sleeping Mind is that the RTR felt it was an overpowered
card, and therefore reduced it to wallpaper. (It's clear to me
that the main intent of Sleeping Mind was to circumvent Wakes, since
the only other ability the card has (at superior, 'Vampires may not
untap during this action') applies to only a few cards - Rat's Warning,
Second Tradition being the ones that spring to mind - *and* only
works at superior.)

Josh

Messages.Author: Joshua Duffin
Messages.Body:
LSJ (vte...@wizards.com) wrote:

[re: cat's guidance]

: This has nothing to do with the current rulings. Cat's Guidance, inferior,

: is useless without the 'usable by a tapped vampire' erratum.

: When played by an untapped vampire (as reaction cards generally are), the
: 'untap this vampire' has no effect. This is true regardless of whether
: the card is played before or after combat.

: And (the good part): it isn't overpowered if it is allowed to work the
: way it was intended.

: So errata (a correction) was issued.

Oh, yeah. Good point. (Interesting that it wasn't issued until recently
though.)

[re: sleeping mind]

: Yes, it would be overpowered if errata was issued to make it function

: as it was almost certainly intended to function. So no errata was
: issued.

Well, there's an entry in the 7/7 rulings, which says that cards played
after Sleeping Mind are allowed to break the rules that Sleeping Mind
attempts to impose.

The RT's position seems to be that Sleeping Mind, as written,
didn't do anything because cards played later were inherently able
circumvent the 'The chosen [tapped] vampire cannot attempt
to block this action' effect. But it seems to me that, given what
the card says, it is clearly preventing that tapped vampire from
blocking even if it could somehow gain the ability to block (eg
with Wake or Forced Awakening).

The superior, which says that tapped vampires can't block the action,
means to me that even if they somehow have the ability to block
despite being tapped (eg by having used a Wake), they are not allowed
to block. Claiming that Wake's use of the phrase "as if untapped"
gets around this because untapped vamps can block as normal is, in
my opinion, a very dubious line of reasoning. A Woken vampire is
still tapped. Therefore a Woken vamp trying to block *is* a tapped
vampire attempting to block the action, which is what Sleeping Mind
prevents tapped vampires from doing.

The argument that Sleeping Mind's effect is applied only when the
card is played, ie that it removes the ability of tapped vampires
to block, which they couldn't do anyway, seems implausible to me.
The card is an action modifier; hence it modifies the action. It's
at least as logical to claim that it gives the action the attribute
'This action cannot be blocked by tapped vampires.' (at superior)

I have no particular problem with the RT's desire to alter Sleeping
Mind in this fashion, but I feel that it certainly should require at
least a ruling, if not errata. (Which is to say, I feel that the
reasoning presented in the 7/7 rulings is weak and should be altered.)

Josh

always the devil's advocate

du...@newton.ruph.cornell.edu (Joshua Duffin) wrote:
> [re: sleeping mind]

>
> Well, there's an entry in the 7/7 rulings, which says that cards played
> after Sleeping Mind are allowed to break the rules that Sleeping Mind
> attempts to impose.
>
> The RT's position seems to be that Sleeping Mind, as written,
> didn't do anything because cards played later were inherently able
> circumvent the 'The chosen [tapped] vampire cannot attempt
> to block this action' effect.

The chosen vampire is not prevented from attempting to block the action.
Superior SM doesn't "choose" any vampires. It merely says that tapped
vampires cannot block. Which was true before SM was played.

Wakey allows the vampire to attempt to block "as if untapped", and SM doesn't
prevent untapped vampires from attempting to block.

Inferior SM says that the chosen vampire cannot block - so not even wakey
can be used to get around that restriction.

> The superior, which says that tapped vampires can't block the action,
> means to me that even if they somehow have the ability to block
> despite being tapped (eg by having used a Wake), they are not allowed
> to block. Claiming that Wake's use of the phrase "as if untapped"
> gets around this because untapped vamps can block as normal is, in
> my opinion, a very dubious line of reasoning. A Woken vampire is
> still tapped. Therefore a Woken vamp trying to block *is* a tapped
> vampire attempting to block the action, which is what Sleeping Mind
> prevents tapped vampires from doing.

And if you played Wakey to play a Deflection? Would that be a tapped
vampire attempting to play a reaction card (and thus not be allowed
since tapped vampires cannot play reaction cards)?

> The argument that Sleeping Mind's effect is applied only when the
> card is played, ie that it removes the ability of tapped vampires
> to block, which they couldn't do anyway, seems implausible to me.
> The card is an action modifier; hence it modifies the action. It's
> at least as logical to claim that it gives the action the attribute
> 'This action cannot be blocked by tapped vampires.' (at superior)

Plausible, yes. Which is why a ruling was issued.

> I have no particular problem with the RT's desire to alter Sleeping
> Mind in this fashion, but I feel that it certainly should require at
> least a ruling, if not errata. (Which is to say, I feel that the
> reasoning presented in the 7/7 rulings is weak and should be altered.)

A ruling was issued.

LSJ (vte...@wizards.com) wrote:

[I wrote]

: > My argument here

: > is that Sleeping Mind, as an action modifier, gives that action the
: > property of not being blockable by tapped vampires, even if they
: > would otherwise be able to block the action.

: Which is true in general.

: Sleeping Mind (superior) states this rule. That changes nothing, since the
: rule is a general rule, given in the rulebook.

I think the rule in the rulebook is essentially 'Only untapped vampires
can be declared as blockers.' I don't think that's the same as 'Tapped
vampires may not block.'

Your interpretation seems to be that Wake with Evening's Freshness uses
the phrase 'as though untapped' in a very meaningful way. That is, it's
not just describing how it is that the Waking vamp could be able to
do stuff while tapped; it's actually giving the vamp the property
'as though untapped' until the end of the action. Wake could have said
simply 'Usable only by a tapped vampire. This vampire can play reaction
cards and attempt to block until the current action is concluded." In
that case, it wouldn't override Sleeping Mind. Right?

But that's not exactly how I'm approaching it...

: *If* SM gives the action the property of not being blockable by tapped
: vampires, and a vampire uses a Wakey to attempt to block "as if untapped",
: then he can attempt to block, unless he could not have attempted to

: block even if he was untapped (due to a Seduction, Blood Bond, Videotape,

: or whatever). Since he is attempting to block "as if untapped", then
: the restriction against blocking while tapped doesn't apply, since he is

: performing as if he is not tapped.

To me, it seems that a Waking vampire (although it is allowed to do
things that normally only untapped vampires can do) is still
undeniably a tapped vampire. It can block and play reaction cards
'as though untapped', but it has not *actually* become untapped. When
the game looks at the Waking vampire and examines its attributes,
it is 'tapped', not 'untapped.'

Therefore, if SM gave the action the property 'unblockable by tapped
vampires', a Waking vampire would still be unable to block, because
the unblockability only cares about the actual status of the vampire
that wants to block - it doesn't care if the vampire can do things
as if it had the opposite status.

: > Well, yes. I just didn't like the reasoning that arrived at it. ;-)

: If errata had been necessary to achieve balance, it would have been issued.
: However, the situation was ambiguous enough to allow a ruling to suffice.

Probably so.

Josh

OK. "Only X may do Y" is equivalent to "NotX cannot do Y" in my book,
and "untapped" is exactly "not tapped". But whichever. If it's vague,
the ruling serves to clarify the ambiguity.

> Your interpretation seems to be that Wake with Evening's Freshness uses
> the phrase 'as though untapped' in a very meaningful way. That is, it's
> not just describing how it is that the Waking vamp could be able to

No, just inasfar as "us[ing] reaction cards and attempt[ing] to block" are
concerned (card text).

> Wake could have said
> simply 'Usable only by a tapped vampire. This vampire can play reaction
> cards and attempt to block until the current action is concluded." In
> that case, it wouldn't override Sleeping Mind. Right?

Possibly.

> But that's not exactly how I'm approaching it...

> undeniably a tapped vampire. It can block and play reaction cards
> 'as though untapped', but it has not *actually* become untapped. When
> the game looks at the Waking vampire and examines its attributes,
> it is 'tapped', not 'untapped.'

A tapped vampire is not untapped. And an untapped vampire is not tapped.
"tapped" and "untapped" are two mutually exclusive states.

Since the vampire can "attempt to block as though untapped", and he could
attempt to block if he were untapped (Sleeping Mind doesn't restrict the
block attempts of untapped vampires), then he can attempt to block.

He is not a tapped vampire attempting to block.
He's a vampire attempting to block as though untapped.

As far as the block attempt is concerned, he's operating exactly as
he would if he were untapped. That is: not tapped.

> Therefore, if SM gave the action the property 'unblockable by tapped
> vampires', a Waking vampire would still be unable to block, because
> the unblockability only cares about the actual status of the vampire
> that wants to block - it doesn't care if the vampire can do things
> as if it had the opposite status.

Possibly.

LSJ (vte...@wizards.com) wrote:
: du...@newton.ruph.cornell.edu (Joshua Duffin) wrote:
: >
: > I think the rule in the rulebook is essentially 'Only untapped vampires

: > can be declared as blockers.' I don't think that's the same as 'Tapped
: > vampires may not block.'

: OK. "Only X may do Y" is equivalent to "NotX cannot do Y" in my book,
: and "untapped" is exactly "not tapped". But whichever. If it's vague,
: the ruling serves to clarify the ambiguity.

"Only X may do Y" is basically equivalent to 'NotX cannot do Y." What
I'm trying to get at is that the wording disparities here don't lend
themselves to such direct equivalencies. Sleeping Mind's text "tapped
minions cannot block this action" is not an exact restatement (even
in reverse) of 'To block, declare one of your untapped vampires as
blocking and tap him' (which is what the VTES rulebook seems to say).

I agree that 'untapped' is the same as 'not tapped'. I think where
I'm having trouble is with 'as though' and exactly how blocking works.

This is why I think that Sleeping Mind's superior is trying to look
at the tapped/untapped status of any minion that might want to block,
at the moment at which they want to block. (That is, since the
"tapped minions cannot block" text is not a direct rulebook quote,
and since it is not parenthetical, it seems to me that it must be
meaningful, and this is what it looks like it means.)

: A tapped vampire is not untapped. And an untapped vampire is not tapped.

: "tapped" and "untapped" are two mutually exclusive states.

Yes, exactly.

: Since the vampire can "attempt to block as though untapped", and he could

: attempt to block if he were untapped (Sleeping Mind doesn't restrict the
: block attempts of untapped vampires), then he can attempt to block.

: He is not a tapped vampire attempting to block.
: He's a vampire attempting to block as though untapped.

This doesn't sound at all like it follows from what you said about
tapped vs. untapped above. As far as I can see, the tapped state of
the waking vampire has in no way been altered to untapped. What has
happened is that Wake is breaking the rules about tapped vampires being
able to block or play reaction cards - it is saying that this Waking
vampire can block or play reactions as though it were untapped.

So it seems to me that Sleeping Mind should still be able to see that
the vampire is actually tapped, and would then prohibit him from blocking.

Sure, the Waking vampire could attempt to block if he were untapped.
But the Waking vampire is not an untapped vampire. He is
a vampire who can block as though untapped. The only way I can see
the Sleeping Mind failing is if Wake's 'as though untapped' property
is so broad that cards looking at the Waking vampire think that it
is actually untapped. And I don't think Wake should be read
that way.

: As far as the block attempt is concerned, he's operating exactly as

: he would if he were untapped. That is: not tapped.

So are you saying that, when you want to Wake and block, you should
physically untap the vampire card, declare the block, and then tap
the card? I would find that disturbing. (I don't think that's where
you're going with this, but it could be. It's always seemed to me
that a Waking vampire was operating very differently from how he
would if he were in fact untapped.)

: > Therefore, if SM gave the action the property 'unblockable by tapped

: > vampires', a Waking vampire would still be unable to block, because
: > the unblockability only cares about the actual status of the vampire
: > that wants to block - it doesn't care if the vampire can do things
: > as if it had the opposite status.

: Possibly.

As long as SM is examining the actual tapped/untapped status, and Wake
doesn't change actual tapped/untapped-ness, I can't see how it could
be otherwise.

Josh

> THEN the vampire blocks.

The vampire Wakes then attempts to block "as if untapped".

> So would a vampire playing Wake untap from a
> Change of Target?

No, since the vampire was tapped before the block, attempted to block
as if untapped, and so is not untapped by Change of Target.

The quoted statement "cards looking at the Waking vampire think that it
is actually untapped" is not the official interpretation.

> And, if Wake is making a vampire untapped so that it can break The
> Sleeping Mind's rules, exactly how does it break *this* part of the
> text?
>
> Card Title: Sleeping Mind, The
> Blood/Pool: 1 blood
> Clan/Discip.: Dominate
> Card Type: Action Modifier
> Card Text: Only usable when the acting vampire's action is
> announced. Choose a tapped vampire. The chosen
> vampire cannot attempt to block this action.
> (S) Only usable when the acting vampire's action is
> announced. Minions cannot untap during this action,
> ^^^^^^^ ^^^^^^ ^^^^^ ^^^^^^ ^^^^ ^^^^^^
> and tapped minions cannot block this action.

It doesn't. The woken vampire doesn't untap - he merely is able to block
as if he were untapped (card text).

I think this is the heart of what I was not getting. I've been
assuming that there is a system of interaction for all cards in
Jyhad; that they basically do things by looking at their own properties,
the properties of other cards, and the properties of effects (actions,
etc) and then modifying or altering those properties. So I figured
that Sleeping Mind produced its superior effect by giving the action
it modified the property "Cannot be blocked by tapped vampires." Then,
that meant that if a Waking vampire tried to block, the action would
look at him and say, "No, you're a tapped vampire, you can't block
this action."

You seem to be saying that it doesn't work that way at all. Can I

with the Rules Outline as a guide to how things are supposed to

1) There is no "waking vamp" before wake is played.

2) Tapped minions have been excluded from blocking this action.
This exclusion is (redundantly) added "before" the wake can be
played. Redundant, since this restriction is true even for actions
which are not modified by superior Sleeping Mind.

Any of those tapped vampires who could've blocked the action
had they been untapped can use Wakey to attempt to block, since
Wakey explicitly allows the reacting vampire to "attempt to block
as though [he were] untapped" (card text).

LSJ (vte...@wizards.com) wrote:

: Which it already had, by the rules on blocking.

My view was that the rules on blocking define what vampires may
be declared as blockers under normal conditions. If Sleeping Mind added
to its action the property 'Cannot be blocked by tapped vampires',
that would impose an additional qualification that a vampire that wanted
to block would have to meet. (My take on it was that this property
would care about the true state of the vampire card that wanted to
block, rather than whether the vampire had the ability to block 'as
though untapped.')

: > Then,

: > that meant that if a Waking vampire tried to block, the action would
: > look at him and say, "No, you're a tapped vampire, you can't block
: > this action."

: The action would "look at him", for purposes of deciding if he could
: block, as an untapped vampire, since Wakey causes him to be treated as
: untapped for purposes of blocking, and say "you can block".

To me, it seems that the action doesn't 'look at him' at all. Instead
the controlling methuselah says, 'This vampire wants to block. Since
he's got a Wake that says he can block as though untapped, Sleeping Mind
can't tell that he's actually tapped. Too bad for Sleeping Mind.'

In other words, the action 'gets fooled' because it doesn't actually
check the vampire's attributes.

: > You seem to be saying that it doesn't work that way at all. Can I

: > ask what the underlying mechanisms are for how Jyhad works? Or is
: > it currently set up as sort of a results-based system,
: > with the Rules Outline as a guide to how things are supposed to
: > work out?

: Not to be snide, but it's just a base-rules-plus-card-text system.
: I'm afraid there is no better answer (or I fail to understand your
: question).

: The Rules Outline is modelled after the base rules. The Outline
: doesn't supercede or correct the actual rules in any way (except
: to follow existsing errata issued on the base rules, of course).

I guess what I was looking for is a better way of thinking about
how cards produce the effects they do. Base rules plus card text
seems to essentially describe what happens, but not how or why it
happens. In other words, there appears to be no rhyme or reason to
the way cards interact, because there is no underlying system that
describes how they're supposed to interact.
